scene: A fisherman and a market vendor stand talking in a flat rice paddy, both alive and unhurried, the horizon dead level behind them.
teaches: A syllable that ends alive is a mid tone for low and mid class alike — the two agree here, which is why they share the scene.
prompt: A fisherman in a conical straw hat and rolled-up trousers and a market vendor in a flat straw hat and a work apron standing and talking in a flooded green rice paddy, both upright, unhurt and relaxed, the horizon a dead flat line behind them under a wide open sky.
narration: The rice paddy. [pause] A fisherman has walked up from the harbour and a market vendor has come out from town, and the two of them are standing in the middle of the field talking, in no hurry at all. [pause] The paddy runs flat to the horizon behind them, and their voices run just as flat — opening level, holding level, finishing level. [pause] A syllable that ends alive — one finishing on a vowel or on a soft ending — comes out mid tone for a low-class letter and for a mid-class letter alike. [pause] When you see those two standing in a flat field, read the syllable flat.

scene: A monk walks down into a dip and then climbs a long hill path, alive and steady, robes bright against the slope.
teaches: High class is the one exception when the syllable ends alive: it rises where the others stay level.
prompt: A monk in an orange robe with a shaved head walking up a long steep hill path, seen from below, the path dipping in the foreground and then rising sharply to a high ridge against the sky.
narration: The hill path. [pause] The monk sets out from the temple on his own, and the path drops into a dip before it climbs, so he goes down a little first and then up and up, his robes bright against the slope. [pause] His voice does what his feet do — down at the start, climbing the whole rest of the way. [pause] A high-class letter, on a syllable that ends alive, rises. [pause] The fisherman and the vendor stayed flat in their field; the monk is walking uphill. So when a high-class letter opens a syllable that ends alive, take your voice down and then up.

scene: A fisherman on a rooftop is killed instantly by a single lightning strike — one flash, already over.
teaches: Low class, dead syllable, short vowel: high tone. Length only ever matters here.
prompt: A fisherman in a conical straw hat and rolled-up trousers standing on the flat roof of a building, at the instant a jagged white lightning bolt hits him. His body arches backwards, arms flung wide, a blinding flash at the point of impact.
narration: The rooftop. [pause] The fisherman has climbed up to fix a tile, and a single bolt of lightning takes him — one flash, over before the sound reaches the street. [pause] It is the quickest end anything meets in this palace, and it happens at the very top of the house. [pause] A low-class letter, a dead syllable, a short vowel: high tone. [pause] This is the one place in the whole system where the length of the vowel decides the answer, so find the vowel first and then read.

scene: The same fisherman goes over a waterfall and drowns slowly in the pool below, the fall drawn out and unhurried.
teaches: Low class, dead syllable, long vowel: falling. The slow death is the long vowel.
prompt: A fisherman in a conical straw hat and rolled-up trousers sinking slowly beneath the surface of a deep green pool at the foot of a tall waterfall, arms drifting upward above him, a long trail of bubbles rising to the light.
narration: The waterfall. [pause] The same fisherman, a different day. This time the river has him, and he goes over the lip and down the long drop into the pool below, and it takes a while. [pause] He starts at the top and finishes at the bottom, with the whole length of the fall in between. [pause] A low-class letter, a dead syllable, a long vowel: falling tone. [pause] Same man, same class, same dead syllable as the rooftop — the vowel got longer and the tone came down with it. Hear the length, and let your voice fall the distance.

scene: A market vendor and a monk both fall down the same well and do not come back up.
teaches: Dead syllable, mid or high class: low tone, and the vowel's length changes nothing. Four rules, one well.
prompt: A market vendor in a flat straw hat and a work apron and a monk in an orange robe with a shaved head falling head-first down a round stone well shaft, arms and legs flailing above them, seen from inside the well looking up at the bright circular opening.
narration: The well. [pause] The market vendor and the monk are both leaning over the same rim, and both of them go in — down the shaft, into the dark, and the dark keeps them. [pause] A well is the one place you have to look down into, which is where a low tone sits. [pause] A dead syllable under a mid-class or a high-class letter gives a low tone. [pause] Four rules end in this well. The vowel's length changes nothing for either class, so short or long, mid or high, they all go down the same shaft.

scene: A one-pointed spear stands driven into the well's rim, and the market vendor and the monk are already gone down the shaft.
teaches: Mai ek over mid or high class: low tone. The one-pointed spear is the mark, and it decides the tone whatever the syllable was doing.
prompt: A plain one-pointed spear standing upright, driven into the stone rim of a round well. A market vendor in a flat straw hat and a work apron and a monk in an orange robe with a shaved head tumbling down the dark shaft beside it, arms above their heads, seen from the well mouth looking down.
narration: The well again, and now there is a spear. [pause] One shaft, one point, driven into the rim and left standing there — and the vendor and the monk are already down in the dark below it. [pause] Count the points: one. Mai ek is the first of the four tone marks, and one point is how you will know it. [pause] Mai ek over a mid-class or a high-class letter gives a low tone. [pause] The spear settles it. Alive, dead, short, long — once that mark is written, the answer comes from the mark.

scene: A two-pronged spear pitches the market vendor and the monk over the lip of the waterfall together.
teaches: Mai tho over mid or high class: falling. Two prongs, two.
prompt: A market vendor in a flat straw hat and a work apron and a monk in an orange robe with a shaved head falling head-first over the lip of a tall waterfall, upside down in the white water. A large two-pronged spear is planted at the clifftop above them, both prongs clearly visible against the sky.
narration: The waterfall, and a spear with two prongs. [pause] It comes in from behind and pitches the vendor and the monk over the lip together, the pair of them going down the drop side by side. [pause] Two prongs. Mai tho is the second mark, and two is what you count. [pause] Mai tho over a mid-class or a high-class letter gives a falling tone. [pause] The same two people as the well, a different spear, and this one sent them over the edge instead of down the shaft.

scene: The same one-pointed spear sends the fisherman over the waterfall instead of into the well.
teaches: Mai ek over low class: falling, not low. The same spear, a different end — low class takes the marks its own way.
prompt: A fisherman in a conical straw hat and rolled-up trousers falling head-first over the lip of a tall waterfall. A plain one-pointed spear is planted at the clifftop above him, its single point sharp against the sky.
narration: The waterfall, and the one-pointed spear is back. [pause] This time it is the fisherman it finds, and instead of standing him at a well rim it sends him straight over the falls. [pause] One point, mai ek — the same mark that put the vendor and the monk down the well. [pause] Mai ek over a low-class letter gives a falling tone. [pause] The mark is the one you already know; the class is what changed the ending. Read the mark, then read the class, and answer from the two of them together.

scene: A two-pronged spear lifts the fisherman up onto the rooftop and leaves him there.
teaches: Mai tho over low class: high. Hauled up where the other two were dragged down.
prompt: A fisherman in a conical straw hat and rolled-up trousers lying sprawled on a flat rooftop against the sky, a large two-pronged spear planted upright on the roof beside him, both prongs clearly visible.
narration: The rooftop, and the two-pronged spear. [pause] It hooks the fisherman under the arms and lifts him — up past the eaves and onto the roof, where it sets him down and leaves him standing there. [pause] Two prongs, mai tho. [pause] Mai tho over a low-class letter gives a high tone. [pause] That same spear dragged the vendor and the monk over a waterfall. Under a low-class letter it hauls upward instead, so the class is what tells you which direction.

scene: The market vendor stands alone on the rooftop holding a trident, its three points against the sky.
teaches: Mai tri only ever sits on mid class, and gives high. Three prongs, and tri is three.
prompt: A market vendor in a flat straw hat and a work apron standing alone on a flat rooftop, holding a large three-pronged trident upright in both hands, its three points sharp and clear against an open sky. Nobody else on the roof.
narration: The rooftop again, and the vendor is up there on his own, holding a trident with its three points against the sky. [pause] Three. Mai tri — tri is three in Thai the way it is three in English, and the three points are up on the roof. [pause] Mai tri over a mid-class letter gives a high tone. [pause] He is alone up there because mai tri only ever sits on a mid-class letter. Seeing that mark answers the class question for you.

scene: The market vendor carries a four-tined pitchfork up the hill path, climbing alone.
teaches: Mai chattawa only ever sits on mid class, and gives rising. Four tines, and chattawa is four.
prompt: A market vendor in a flat straw hat and a work apron climbing alone up a steep hill path, holding up a single four-tined wooden pitchfork, exactly four straight tines spread wide and clear against the open sky.
narration: The hill path, and the vendor is climbing it with a four-tined pitchfork over his shoulder. [pause] Four tines. Mai chattawa is the fourth mark, and chattawa is four. [pause] Mai chattawa over a mid-class letter gives a rising tone. [pause] He is walking the monk's path, dipping at the start and climbing all the rest of the way, and his voice goes with him. [pause] Like mai tri, this mark only ever lands on a mid-class letter, so seeing it settles the class.
